newsitem.title: CAMBODIA: Cambodia to ask Thais to find rebel hardliners.
newsitem.headline: Cambodia to ask Thais to find rebel hardliners.

text.p: Cambodian co-Premiers Prince Norodom Ranariddh and Hun Sen were expected to ask Bangkok to help find key Khmer Rouge hardline leaders who might have crossed into Thailand, officials said on Thursday.

The government fears Khmer Rouge defence chief Son Sen and Nuon Chea, right-hand man of hardline leader Pol Pot, could have crossed into Thailand with commander Nikorn after dissident Khmer Rouge guerrillas took over the hardliner's key Samlaut base on Monday.

"Hun Sen has signed a letter and sent it to the first Prime Minister (Ranariddh) late last night and hopes the prince will sign today before sending it to the Thai government to ask for their intervention," said a Hun Sen aide, without elaborating.

"We are not sure where they escaped to," Defence Minister Tea Banh said of the Khmer Rouge hardliners. "We only know that they have left the captured area. Thus the royal government can contact the Thai government to ask for their help."
Thai military sources at the border said they had not heard of any hardline guerrillas escaping into Thailand.
Senior Thai diplomats in Phnom Penh were unavailable for comment.

But dissident Khmer Rouge officials loyal to Ieng Sary said when contacted by telephone at their border base of Pailin on Thursday that Nuon Chea and Son Sen had escaped through Thailand to their northern rebel Cambodian Anlong Veng stronghold.
Ieng Sary and a large number of other dissident Khmer Rouge rebels broke away from the hardline group in August.

An aide to Pailin commander Ei Chien said they had received the news on Tuesday and said that they were hunting for Son Sen's younger brother Nikorn, who was believed to be still hiding with his followers in jungle on the Cambodian side.
Guerrillas from divisions led by Ei Chien and other breakaway Khmer Rouge commanders on Monday took control of northwestern Samlaut military base from Pol Pot loyalists.

Defence Ministry officials said that in addition to the base, a further 2,000 fighters and thousands of dependents had since defected to the dissident Khmer Rouge faction of Ieng Sary, foreign minister during the brutal 1975-79 Khmer Rouge rule.

Ieng Sary, pardoned last month from a 1979 death sentence for his role in the deaths of more than one million people under Pol Pot's "killing fields" rule, broke with the hardliners in August and forged a ceasefire with the government.

His commanders and the coalition government have been discussing a full merger of their forces and opening up the guerrilla areas, but Ei Chien told Reuters from Pailin on Wednesday that they had not yet reached a full agreement.
Military analysts, however, said the loss of Samlaut would be a blow to the hardliners as it removed their only toehold in the area controlled by the dissidents.
Anlong Veng remains their most important stronghold but the hardliners also have influence in the southwest.
